b: I’m having an issue with navigating a new “skipping lunch” habit.

I was recently diagnosed with ADHD and am now on medication. It’s a mixed bag, as it helps me focus but I’ve found that the only thing that works to manage side effects is to not eat at all during the workday and get my nutritional needs covered during dinners and weekends. But food is just so ingrained culturally that it’s leading to awkward situations.

At the office, I’ve tried sliding in at the lunch table with only a cup of tea (people notice and keep offering me half their own lunch), skipping lunch entirely (people express worry about my workload), finding an excuse to run an errand around lunch time (I miss having a break and catching up), simply saying, “Oh I’m not hungry right now” and visibly eating something around 5 pm so they don’t worry about me (feels performative, and 5 pm is on the early side for me still).

I am a coach/consultant of sorts and meet with a lot of committees in schools and associations. These are friendly people who like to offer me cookies, coffee, pastries, and fruits. I seem to keep coming off as out of step with their social norm. I tend to just cheerily go “not for me thank you” or “oh no thanks, I had a big breakfast” or tell them I’m really only hankering for a cup of tea, but I get confusion, pitiful looks, or people rummaging around in their staff room kitchens for other things to offer me.
I’m not sure I want to be “out” with everyone or mention medication. I get to know these associates over 10 or so meetings but we’re not quite friends.

My co-workers have guessed about the ADHD just from how I am, even before my official diagnosis. But I am still getting used to the meds situation, so I have only told my supervisor. We have a super open culture so I probably will talk about it eventually, but I can’t help but feel there will be more stigma attached to the medication than the disability.
Do you have any guidance on how to deal with all this weirdness? Stock phrases I can keep on hand?
You can read my answer to this letter at New York Magazine.
